rationale: A wins because it knows where the story stops. It refuses the fake competitor play in "On takes on Nike and Adidas with its subscription model," while B smuggles the same temptation back in as "does the rest of the running category have to follow?" A's "On Is a Publicly Traded Company That Just Launched a Subscription Shoe. It Has Not Disclosed the Economics" is a real reporter-shaped angle with a pressure point; B has a terrific line in "it won't say how big the loop is," but pads the set with weaker speculation.
gaps_in_A: "Consumer mail-back programs in other categories have historically struggled with low return rates" is not in the update. Make that a proof target, not a stated fact.
"whether the circular economy has found a scalable business model" leans into broad think-piece language. The reporter hook is sharper when tied to On's missing pilot return and recovery data.

A underplays the clean ESG-accountability angle around "recycling-rate ... not disclosed." It circles the issue in category and materials angles but does not make the data gap its own strongest sustainability story.
gaps_in_B: "moving a core product line to this model" is invented. The update says Cyclon is a running shoe, not that it is a core product line.
"does the rest of the running category have to follow?" is competitor-pressure fan fiction without market-share data, rival response, or evidence incumbents care.
"does a nationwide rollout prove shoppers will accept access-not-ownership" overclaims the evidence. A launch tests behavior; it does not prove acceptance.
The next step, "Pick one angle, then use find-journalists," punts on strategy. A founder needs the editor to choose the strongest lane, not admire six doors.
